questions.question: Classical Sunni scholars Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi identify the 'sa'il' (supplicant) in the opening verse as which figure who mockingly demanded punishment?
options: A. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb
B. Nadr ibn al-Harith
C. Walid ibn al-Mughira
D. Umayyah ibn Khalaf
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi identify the questioner as Nadr ibn al-Harith, a Meccan opponent who sarcastically demanded proof of the punishment the Prophet warned about. His challenge links to Surah al-Anfal 8:32, and he was later executed at Badr — which Sunni scholars view as a worldly fulfilment of the very punishment he had mocked.

questions.question: True or false: The Arabic word 'waqi'' used in verse 1 to describe the punishment means it is merely possible, not certain.
questions.explanation: The term 'waqi'' means 'bound to happen' — inevitable. From the very first verse the surah establishes that the punishment is absolutely certain, a matter of 'when' not 'if.' As the tafsir explains, mocking the warning does not prevent it; it only increases accountability.

questions.question: According to Imam al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, what does 'a Day the measure of which is fifty thousand years' in verse 4 primarily describe?
options: A. The age of the universe at the time of the Quran's revelation
B. The duration of the Day of Judgment as experienced by those suffering through it
C. The time required for the angels to construct the heavens
D. The lifespan of paradise after the Last Day
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari records the dominant opinion — traced to Ibn Abbas — that the fifty thousand years refers to the enormous duration of the Day of Judgment. Ibn Kathir affirms this, noting that for the disbeliever that Day will be experienced as fifty thousand years of anguish, whereas multiple hadith confirm it will pass for the sincere believer as briefly as the time between two prayers.

questions.question: True or false: Sunni classical scholars, including Imam al-Qurtubi, consider the majority view to be that 'al-Ruh' mentioned alongside the angels in verse 4 refers to the Angel Jibreel.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi lists the scholarly positions on 'al-Ruh' and finds the identification with Jibreel most strongly supported by the weight of hadith evidence. Tafsir al-Jalalayn likewise confirms this identification, with Jibreel named separately from the angels to indicate his supreme rank among the angelic creation.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb in 'Fi Zilal al-Quran' uses the fifty-thousand-year figure in verse 4 to make which point about the Meccan disbelievers who demanded immediate punishment?
options: A. They operated on a purely human scale of time, which this verse shatters completely
B. They understood the cosmic scale of divine justice but refused to believe in it
C. They correctly calculated that the Day was still fifty thousand years away
D. They feared the Day but disguised their fear as mockery
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran observes that when the Meccan mockers demanded immediate punishment they were thinking within a purely human framework of time. The verse demolishes that framework: the Day of Judgment is not an extension of human time but a cosmic event of proportions that dwarfs all of human history, operating on a scale the mockers could not comprehend.

questions.question: What does the Arabic word 'halu'an' in verse 19 describe about the default state of human nature?
options: A. A tendency toward laziness when faced with responsibility
B. An excessive emotional reactivity: panic in hardship and stinginess in ease
C. A natural inclination toward generosity that faith must discipline
D. A peaceful contentment that only turns sour when disturbed by others
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari records from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that 'halu'' describes extreme emotional reactivity: when something unpleasant happens the person falls into despair, and when something pleasant happens they become stingy. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi adds that 'halu'' describes the soul's natural condition of dependence and need, which produces anxiety and its downstream moral consequences when not oriented toward Allah.

questions.question: True or false: In verse 20, the Quran says the anxious person panics only when evil 'overwhelms' them, meaning only major disasters trigger this reaction.
questions.explanation: The verse uses 'massa,' meaning 'touches' or 'reaches' — not 'overwhelms.' This is deliberate: even minor hardships suffice to produce extreme panic in the person without spiritual grounding. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi notes this word choice reveals the spiritual fragility of a life not anchored in faith and trust in Allah.

questions.question: Ibn Kathir treats verses 19-21 as a unified passage. What relationship does he identify between panic in adversity (v.20) and stinginess in prosperity (v.21)?
options: A. They are independent vices that happen to affect the same person by coincidence
B. They are twin expressions of the single root condition of 'halu'' — anxious human nature without faith
C. Stinginess causes anxiety, making them sequential rather than simultaneous
D. Panic in adversity is a sin while stinginess is merely a character flaw
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir treats verses 19-21 as inseparable: the one who turns away from divine guidance turns toward wealth as a substitute source of security. Imam al-Qurtubi confirms that panic in adversity and stinginess in prosperity are not independent vices but twin expressions of the same underlying condition of halu' — restless anxiety rooted in the absence of faith.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli argues that verse 19's description of 'halu'' (human anxiety) is a condemnation of human nature as inherently defective.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir explicitly states that the verse presents halu' not as a condemnation but as a description of a starting condition that faith is designed to address. The surah's movement from halu' in verse 19 to the believers' qualities in verses 22-35 is a map of the journey from anxious default to faithful stability.

questions.question: Why does the Quran call the portion in believers' wealth a 'known right' (haqqun ma'lum) rather than a 'generous gift' in verse 24?
options: A. To limit generosity to a fixed amount so believers do not overspend
B. To reframe wealth: a specified portion belongs by right to those in need, not merely at the donor's discretion
C. To establish that only zakat counts as charity and all other giving is optional
D. To show that the poor must formally request their share before the obligation arises
questions.explanation: Calling the portion a 'haqq' (right) rather than a gift fundamentally reframes wealth: a portion of what a believer holds was never entirely theirs to keep. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes this as a moral revolution — it removes the donor's psychological leverage over the recipient and establishes giving as an act of justice rather than patronage.

questions.question: True or false: According to classical Sunni tafsir, 'al-mahrum' (the deprived) in verse 25 refers only to people who openly beg in public.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari records narrations from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid identifying 'al-mahrum' as a person in genuine need who does not or cannot make that need known through asking — the dignified poor, those prevented from begging by pride or circumstance. Imam al-Qurtubi notes that naming both 'al-sa'il' and 'al-mahrum' creates a positive obligation on believers to actively seek out hidden need rather than waiting for petitions.

questions.question: Verse 34 uses 'yuhafizun' (they maintain/guard) for prayer while verse 23 used 'da'imun' (constant). What extra dimension does 'yuhafizun' add according to Wahbah al-Zuhayli and Ibn Uthaymeen?
options: A. It restricts the prayer obligation to those who are physically healthy
B. It requires extra voluntary prayers alongside the obligatory ones
C. It calls for active guardianship of prayer's times, purity conditions, and quality of heart — not merely regularity
D. It indicates that prayer in congregation is obligatory rather than recommended
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir explains that 'yuhafizun' adds active guardianship: protecting prayer from erosion in its timing, conditions of purity, and interior quality of khushu'. Ibn Uthaymeen similarly taught that 'yuhafizun' encompasses the conditions, pillars, and obligations of prayer — giving Allah what He is owed in worship, not performing salah on autopilot.

questions.question: What is the structural significance of the believers' description in verses 22-34 opening and closing with prayer?
options: A. It shows that prayer is so easy it needs no other virtues to support it
B. It indicates prayer applies only at the beginning and end of a believer's day
C. It frames all other virtues — giving, chastity, trustworthiness — within prayer as the encompassing foundation
D. It suggests the other virtues are optional additions for those who have mastered the five prayers
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim notes that the surah's portrait of believers is literally enclosed within prayer, signalling that prayer is not one item on a list but the encompassing framework of the believing life. He cites the Prophetic hadith in Sahih Muslim: the first thing a servant will be called to account for is their prayer, and if it is sound all other deeds will be sound.

questions.question: True or false: The word 'mukramun' (honored) in verse 35 indicates that the believers' reward in paradise is divine honor and dignity — not merely physical comfort.
questions.explanation: Verse 35 describes the believers as 'mukramun' — honored ones — in gardens of paradise. The tafsir explains that this word signals more than material pleasure: it is divine honor and dignity bestowed on the righteous, the ultimate reward for those who prayed, gave, and maintained patience throughout their lives, standing in contrast to the humiliation awaiting those who mocked and hoarded.

questions.question: As reflected in Ibn Uthaymeen's broader teachings applied in the tafsir, how are the obligations described in verses 22-34 — prayer, charity, moral restraint — best understood in relation to verse 19?
options: A. As optional spiritual extras for advanced believers who have already conquered halu'
B. As punishments imposed on humanity for failing to govern its own nature
C. As remedies specifically prescribed for the condition of halu' — treating a known spiritual disease
D. As cultural practices inherited from previous prophets with no connection to human psychology
questions.explanation: Ibn Uthaymeen observed that the obligations of prayer, charity, and moral restraint in the following verses are not burdens imposed on an otherwise free human being but remedies prescribed for the specific spiritual condition of halu'. The surah's architecture functions as both a diagnosis (verse 19) and a prescription (verses 22-34), showing that Islamic practice is designed to heal the restless, anxious human default.
